content.text:
For Q11 (cost and processing time of EOS from the final rule): I need the RIA figures — fee amounts. Let me grep for "fee" with dollar signs, e.g. "\$[0-9,]+" and "I-539" fee. Also grep "median" or "per-application cost". The RIA is at lines 13151-14528. Grep for "\$" in that range isn't rangeable; grep whole doc for pattern like "\$4[0-9][0-9]" or "fee of". Let me grep pattern "\$[0-9][0-9,]*( fee| per)" — simpler: grep "per application" or "application fee". Also "biometrics" fee $85. Let me grep "\$[0-9]" limited... too many. Try pattern "I-539 fee|fee associated|cost per|per-adjudication|hourly rate". Better: grep "hour" in RIA? Grep "adjudicat.*cost".

Also for Q16(b) early filing: grep "file.*before|in advance" — maybe skip; state rule silent.

Next big items: proclamations, OPT fees NPRM, 60-day grace NPRM, 2026-20955, H-1B fee rulemakings, effective-date-change check (CRA), and RIA fee figures.

Batch next:
1. fr_grep 2026-14439 pattern "\$[0-9,]+(\.[0-9]+)? ?(per|for) (hour|application|adjudication)" hmm complex. Simpler: pattern "I-539" with context 2, max 20 — might show fee mentions. Or grep " USCIS fee|filing fee|fee of \$". Let me try pattern "fee" near "I-539": pattern "I-539.{0,200}fee|fee.{0,200}I-539" — regex across lines? . doesn't match newline. Use pattern "fee[s]? (of|is) \$[0-9]" context 3.

Actually the RIA likely computes cost per EOS application: e.g., "$470 I-539 fee + $85 biometrics + $30 hourly"? Let me grep "\$470|\$420|\$85|\$30 per hour". Pattern: "\$[0-9]{2,3}( |\.|,)" with max 40 too many. Try "per hour" context 4.

content.text:
2026-18631: removes 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) — the 60-day grace period upon cessation of employment for E-1/E-2/E-3/H-1B/H-4/L-1/L-2/O-1/O-3/TC/TN etc. — NOT F-1's 60-day departure period (which for F-1s is in 214.2(f)(5)(v) — 30 days — or the transition 60 days under 214.1(m)(1)). So it doesn't affect Priya's 60 days. Wait — careful: 214.1(l)(2) is the "up to 60-day grace period upon cessation of employment" for certain employment-based nonimmigrants. Priya's 60-day departure period comes from 214.1(m)(1) transition. So (c) no. (d) does it bear on other students? Only students who change to H-1B etc. and then stop working — e.g., Lena (H-1B) after status start? Lena's H-1B start July 1, 2027; if employment ceases, grace period eliminated. Also the 60-day grace in the transition (m)(1) is not touched. Also Tomás? Not F-1 related. Statement: proposal, comments closed Nov 10, 2026, not final, not in force.

Wait — but should double check whether 2026-18631 also touches F-1? CFR affected: 204, 214. 214.1(l)(2) is E/1/E-2 etc. Let me quickly grep 2026-18631 for "F-1" or "214.2(f)" to confirm scope for (d).

2026-20955: ends automatic extension of EAD validity for timely renewal applications in certain categories (8 CFR 274a.12... likely TPS and asylum categories etc.). Does it affect F-1 OPT renewals? F-1 OPT isn't renewable except STEM extension (not a renewal of same EAD). The final rule's CFR affected: 274. Need to check which categories — relevant to Q10: "documents that would matter to an F-1 student planning post-graduation work" — this rule ends automatic 180-day/540-day extensions for renewal EAD categories (TPS, asylum, etc.) — for an F-1 student planning OPT, marginal. But if a student later changes status... It's relevant-ish. I'll check briefly whether F-1 categories are covered — grep "F-1" in 2026-20955.

content.text:
Proclamation 10973: $100,000 payment for petitions for aliens outside the U.S. entering as H-1B; restriction applies only to aliens who enter/attempt to enter after effective date (Sept 21, 2025); expires absent extension 12 months after effective date = Sept 21, 2026. Exception: national interest (Sec. 1(c)); Sec. 2(a): applies to petitions on behalf of aliens outside the U.S.

Lena: F-1 in the U.S., change of status — not entering; petition for beneficiary inside the U.S. Section 1 restriction applies to entry; Sec. 2(b): petitions on behalf of aliens "currently outside the United States". So Lena's COS petition not covered. But could reach her: if she travels abroad and seeks to enter as H-1B, or if the proclamation is extended by the 2026 proclamation. Read 2026-19554 to see what it does (extension? modification?).

    65  Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant 
    66                  Workers

    68                  By the President of the United States of America
    69  
    70                  A Proclamation
    71  
    72                  On September 19, 2025, Proclamation 10973 (Restriction 
    73                  on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers) (2025 
    74                  Proclamation), was issued to address significant abuses 
    75                  of the H-1B nonimmigrant visa program. The restrictions 
    76                  enacted by the 2025 Proclamation have proven to be 
    77                  highly effective but the underlying conditions 
    78                  necessitating the restrictions persist. It is therefore 
    79                  in the interests of the United States to extend the 
    80                  2025 Proclamation for an additional 12 months, until 
    81                  12:00 a.m. eastern daylight time on September 21, 2027.
    82  
    83                  As explained in the 2025 Proclamation, the H-1B 
    84                  nonimmigrant visa program was created to bring 
    85                  temporary workers in high-skilled functions into the 
    86                  United States, but it has been exploited to replace, 
    87                  not supplement, American workers with lower-paid labor. 
    88                  Certain employers, including information technology 
    89                  (IT) staffing and outsourcing firms, have abused the 
    90                  system to suppress wages and displace American workers, 
    91                  and this has both harmed the labor market for American 
    92                  workers while also making it difficult to attract and 
    93                  retain the most highly skilled temporary workers. IT 
    94                  staffing and outsourcing firms were found to supply a 
    95                  large volume of entry-level temporary H-1B workers, 
    96                  generally at a much lower salary compared to full-time, 
    97                  traditional workers, and some of these firms later 
    98                  outsourced IT roles to cheap labor markets overseas. 
    99                  This has led to a proliferation of lower-paid foreign 
   100                  labor flooding the American labor market and making it 
   101                  difficult for American workers and recent graduates, 
   102                  especially in science, technology, engineering, and 
   103                  math (STEM) fields, to find employment.
   104  
   105                  To combat these abuses, the 2025 Proclamation set forth 
   106                  a restriction on entry of certain H-1B nonimmigrant 
   107                  workers, except for those petitions that were 
   108                  accompanied or supplemented by a $100,000 payment, 
   109                  subject to very limited exceptions. The 2025 
   110                  Proclamation went into effect on September 21, 2025, 
   111                  and, since then, the $100,000 payment has been made for 
   112                  over 700 petitions.
   113  
   114                  Additionally, the 2025 Proclamation required initiation 
   115                  of rulemakings by the Department of Homeland Security 
   116                  (DHS) and the Department of Labor (DOL) to address 
   117                  systemic H-1B program concerns. On December 29, 2025, 
   118                  DHS published a final rule, titled Weighted Selection 
   119                  Process for Registrants and Petitioners Seeking to File 
   120                  Cap-Subject H-1B Petitions, 90 Fed. Reg. 60864 (DHS 
   121                  final rule), to address the policy goals consistent 
   122                  with section 4(b) of the 2025 Proclamation. Through 
   123                  this rule, DHS created and implemented a weighted 
   124                  selection process that prioritizes the allocation of 
   125                  visas to higher-skilled and higher-paid aliens to 
   126                  better protect the wages, working conditions, and job 
   127                  opportunities for American workers. This policy better 
   128                  serves the intent of the H-1B statutory scheme, 
   129                  incentivizes employers to recruit temporary workers for 
   130                  roles at the highest pay and skill levels, and was in 
   131                  effect for the Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 H-1B cap season. 
   132                  On March 27, 2026, DOL published a notice of proposed 
   133                  rulemaking, titled Improving Wage Protections for the 
   134                  Temporary and Permanent Employment of Certain Foreign 
   135                  Nationals in the United States, 91 Fed. Reg. 15454,
   136  
   137  [[Page 60498]]
   138  
   139                  to address the policy goals consistent with section 
   140                  4(a) of the 2025 Proclamation. The DOL's analysis of 
   141                  labor condition application data found that the average 
   142                  wage actually paid to H-1B workers, and the prevailing 
   143                  wage assigned to their positions, both remain well 
   144                  below the average wage earned by comparable American 
   145                  workers. The rule, once finalized, will better align 
   146                  prevailing wage levels with wages paid to similarly 
   147                  employed and located American workers and will 
   148                  strengthen overall program integrity. Finally, my 
   149                  Administration continues to explore other complementary 
   150                  efforts that would, among other things, reform the H-1B 
   151                  program and assist with cost-recovery for immigration 
   152                  program administration.
   153  
   154                  Since the effective date of the 2025 Proclamation and 
   155                  subsequent promulgation of the DHS final rule, there 
   156                  have been several measurable impacts on the H-1B 
   157                  program, including a significant reduction in H-1B 
   158                  registrations filed by large IT outsourcing firms, with 
   159                  the largest IT staffing and outsourcing firms reducing 
   160                  their combined H-1B registrations from 24,946 to 2,055, 
   161                  a 92 percent decrease. There has also been a large 
   162                  reduction in consular processing requests, which are 
   163                  used to bring workers into the United States, noting a 
   164                  nearly 97 percent decrease from the FY 2025 to FY 2027 
   165                  cap seasons. Finally, there has been a positive shift 
   166                  in FY 2027 H-1B registration and selection data toward 
   167                  higher-skilled and higher-paid workers, with 
   168                  registrations for beneficiaries with at least a U.S. 
   169                  Master's degree rising from 45.1 percent of total 
   170                  registrants for FY 2026 to 66.1 percent for FY 2027. 
   171                  Job offers with wages corresponding to the two highest 
   172                  wage levels accounted for approximately 46.3 percent of 
   173                  H-1B registration selections while those corresponding 
   174                  with the lowest wage level accounted for only 17.8 
   175                  percent. It is reasonable to conclude that the required 
   176                  $100,000 payment and newly implemented weighted 
   177                  selection process have had the combined effect of 
   178                  deterring low-wage and low-skilled recruitment while 
   179                  increasing access for high-skilled and high-wage 
   180                  workers, as intended by the 2025 Proclamation.
   181  
   182                  Although the 2025 Proclamation and subsequent 
   183                  rulemaking have had the desired effects, the underlying 
   184                  conditions precipitating their issuance persist and, 
   185                  without an extension of the 2025 Proclamation, it is 
   186                  highly likely that progress will halt and program abuse 
   187                  will resume, undermining American workers and posing a 
   188                  threat to the labor market that would be detrimental to 
   189                  the interests of the United States. The 2025 
   190                  Proclamation highlighted a number of concerns, 
   191                  including high unemployment rates for recent graduates, 
   192                  wage suppression, fraud, and national security threats. 
   193                  Currently, these issues continue to undermine our 
   194                  economy, with unemployment rates for recent college 
   195                  graduates standing at 5.7 percent as of June 2026, a 
   196                  marginal decrease from September 2025, when the rate 
   197                  was 5.8 percent. Underemployment for recent college 
   198                  graduates also continues to cause concern, having risen 
   199                  from 41.8 percent in September 2025 to 42 percent as of 
   200                  June 2026. Additionally, while DOL is actively in the 
   201                  process of promulgating a rule to restore integrity to 
   202                  the prevailing wage system, it will take a significant 
   203                  amount of time to correct and balance the labor market. 
   204                  Finally, while fraud and abuse continue to be 
   205                  identified and investigated, these are ongoing and 
   206                  pervasive concerns that require a sustained, 
   207                  comprehensive response reflected in the entry 
   208                  restriction imposed by the 2025 Proclamation.
   209  
   210                  A review of the 2025 Proclamation's impacts and other 
   211                  recent policy changes has shown significant measurable 
   212                  changes in H-1B filing patterns that demonstrate the 
   213                  effectiveness of the 2025 Proclamation and a need for 
   214                  its extension. An extension of the 2025 Proclamation 
   215                  will continue to protect the economic and national 
   216                  security interests of the United States, improve labor 
   217                  market access for American workers and graduates, and 
   218                  ensure that employers recruit only the most highly-
   219                  skilled and essential alien workers when needed in line 
   220                  with the original intent of the program. As a result, 
   221                  the Secretary of State, the Attorney General, the 
   222                  Secretary of Labor, and the Secretary of Homeland 
   223                  Security have jointly recommended an extension of the 
   224                  2025 Proclamation.
   225  
   226  [[Page 60499]]
   227  
   228                  As a result of these reviews and considerations, I have 
   229                  decided to continue to impose the limitations set forth 
   230                  in Proclamation 10973 on the entry into the United 
   231                  States by certain nonimmigrant workers. Accordingly, by 
   232                  the authority vested in me as President by the 
   233                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
   234                  America, it is hereby ordered:
   235  
   236                  Section 1. Restriction on Entry. (a) Pursuant to 
   237                  sections 212(f) and 215(a) of the Immigration and 
   238                  Nationality Act (INA) (8 U.S.C. 1182(f) and 1185(a)), 
   239                  the entry into the United States of aliens as 
   240                  nonimmigrants to perform services in a specialty 
   241                  occupation under section 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) of the INA 
   242                  (8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b)), is restricted, except 
   243                  for those aliens whose petitions are accompanied or 
   244                  supplemented by a payment of $100,000--subject to the 
   245                  exceptions set forth in subsection (c) of this section. 
   246                  This restriction shall expire, absent extension, 12 
   247                  months after the effective date of this proclamation, 
   248                  which shall be 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on 
   249                  September 21, 2026.
   250  
   251                      (b) The Secretary of Homeland Security shall 
   252                  restrict decisions on petitions not accompanied by a 
   253                  $100,000 payment for H-1B specialty occupation workers 
   254                  under section 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) of the INA, who are 
   255                  currently outside the United States, for 12 months 
   256                  following the effective date of this proclamation as 
   257                  set forth in subsection (a) of this section.
   258                      (c) The restriction imposed pursuant to subsections 
   259                  (a) and (b) of this section shall not apply to any 
   260                  individual alien, all aliens working for a company, or 
   261                  all aliens working in an industry, if the Secretary of 
   262                  Homeland Security determines, in the Secretary's 
   263                  discretion, that the hiring of such aliens to be 
   264                  employed as H-1B specialty occupation workers is in the 
   265                  national interest and does not pose a threat to the 
   266                  security or welfare of the United States.
   267  
   268                  Sec. 2. Compliance. (a) Employers shall, prior to 
   269                  filing an H-1B petition on behalf of an alien outside 
   270                  the United States, obtain and retain documentation 
   271                  showing that the payment described in section 1 of this 
   272                  proclamation has been made.
   273  
   274                      (b) The Secretary of State shall verify receipt of 
   275                  payment of the amount described in section 1 of this 
   276                  proclamation during the H-1B visa petition process and 
   277                  shall approve only those visa applications for which 
   278                  the filing employer has made the payment described in 
   279                  section 1 of this proclamation.
   280                      (c) The Department of State and the Department of 
   281                  Homeland Security shall coordinate to take all 
   282                  necessary and appropriate action to implement this 
   283                  proclamation and to deny entry to the United States to 
   284                  any H-1B nonimmigrant for whom the prospective employer 
   285                  has not made the payment described in section 1 of this 
   286                  proclamation.
   287  
   288                  Sec. 3. Scope and Implementation of Restriction on 
   289                  Entry. (a) The restriction on entry pursuant to section 
   290                  1 of this proclamation shall apply only to aliens who 
   291                  enter or attempt to enter the United States after the 
   292                  effective date of this proclamation as set forth in 
   293                  section 1(a) of this proclamation. This restriction 
   294                  applies to aliens who must seek admission to the United 
   295                  States to effectuate the approval of a petition 
   296                  described in section 1 of this proclamation, including 
   297                  through consular notification, notification at a port 
   298                  of entry, pre-flight inspection, or pre-clearance.
   299

content.text:
Also Executive Order 14431 "Enhancing Program Integrity and Interagency Coordination in the Administration of the H-1B Nonimmigrant Visa Program" — in the same FR issue (91 FR 60497 page range includes EO 14431). That's another presidential document bearing on the $100,000 payment (Q7(a) "any other presidential documents that bear on it"). Let me check the EO briefly — it's published in the same FR issue, pages 60500+. Let me search for it: doc number? fr_search for "Enhancing Program Integrity" PRESDOCU.

Also Q7(c): "DHS rulemakings in the Federal Register that would add fees for H-1B petitions" — search for H-1B fee NPRM. The proclamation mentions DOL wage NPRM (not fees) and DHS weighted selection final rule. Maybe there's an H-1B fee NPRM in 2026. Search fr_search "H-1B" fee proposed rule since 2026-01-01.

Try fr_search query "correction" "Fee for Certain H-1B Petitions".

content.text:
EO 14431 doesn't impose the payment; it's program-integrity/coordination. It "bears on" the payment framework in that it's part of the H-1B restriction program.

Remaining gaps:
- Q11: final rule figures for EOS cost and processing time. The RIA: need figures. Grep in 2026-14439 for "I-539" fee amounts like "$470" didn't show. Let me grep "$[0-9]{3} " maybe with words "burden hours" or "per application". Try pattern "per (application|petition|request)|each (application|request)" in RIA region — can't restrict region. Try pattern "burden hours" context 3, or "I-539.{0,120}\$". Let me grep "I-539" with context 2, max 20 — may be too many (many matches). Try pattern "\$[1-9][0-9]{1,3}(\.[0-9]{2})? (per|for) " max 25.

- Q16(b) "How early may she file?" — check EOS comment section G (5745-6984) for timing discussion; maybe commenters asked when to file; response might say "may file at any time before expiration". Grep "before the program end date|prior to the expiration|as early as" in 2026-14439.

- Q15 statement 4: whether ELT medical extension beyond 24 months allowed. Look at response around line 8081-8110 (Response to ELT limits). Read 8081-8160.

- Q5: Mei transfer — graduate-level transfer prohibition: (f)(5)(ii)(A): grad students may not transfer unless SEVP exception for extenuating circumstances. Mei: master's at School A (initial I-20), PhD at School B — higher level. (ii)(B): completing program at one level and beginning higher level = maintaining status. But transfer rules: (f)(8)(i)(C): "The student is not currently in a graduate level program of study, unless an exception has been authorized by SEVP under (f)(5)(ii)(A)." So Mei, currently in a master's (graduate level), cannot transfer unless SEVP authorizes exception. Hmm — but change of education level procedures (f)(8)(iii): "A change of education level can be accomplished according to the transfer procedures outlined in (f)(8)(ii)." She's in a graduate program → transfer barred by (f)(8)(i)(C) unless SEVP exception. But wait — (f)(5)(ii)(B) says a student who has completed a program and begins a new program at a higher level is maintaining status. Does completing the master's then starting PhD count as a change of education level via transfer? (f)(8)(i)(C) bars transfer if "currently in a graduate level program". If Mei completes the master's first (May 14, 2027) and then transfers to School B for the PhD before starting... she'd no longer be "currently" in the program — she'd be a completed student within OPT-less window. Eligibility (f)(8)(i)(B)(2): "Have completed a degree program" → eligible to transfer. So after completion, transfer permitted (also must meet (G): begin classes within 5 months of program completion date — May 14 + 5 months = Oct 14, 2027; PhD starts Aug 23, 2027 → OK). But she must also file EOS since her authorized stay ends (transition: program end May 14, 2027 + 60 days) before PhD start (Aug 23, 2027), and new program end date is beyond authorized admission → EOS required (214.1(m)(1), (f)(8)(iv)). Also Q5 asks: "Is there anything in the rule, or in later Federal Register documents, that could change your conclusion?" — (f)(5)(ii)(E): DHS may delay/suspend (ii)(A)-(C) until Sept 14, 2028 by FR notification/SEVP website — no such notification found in searches. Also the OPT fees NPRM alternative ($70,000 re-applied at higher level) — doesn't affect transfer. Also 60-day grace NPRM doesn't affect transfers.

Also for Q5, identify "every provision in the final regulatory text that bears": (f)(8)(i) intro & (A)-(H), (f)(5)(ii)(A),(B),(C),(D), (f)(8)(ii), (f)(8)(iii), (f)(8)(iv), 214.1(m)(1) (EOS requirement), 214.1(a)(4)(i) if readmission instead.

- Q6 Ahmed: completes master's Dec 11, 2026, wants MBA (same level, master's) in Aug 2027. (f)(5)(ii)(C): after Sept 15, 2026, completed program at one level may not maintain/be admitted/provided F-1 status through program at same or lower level. MBA is same level → barred. Both routes: transfer (f)(8)(i) — also barred since he can't maintain status through same-level program; readmission (a)(4)(i) — CBP can't admit him into same-level program. So (a): No, under either route, unless DHS delays/suspends (ii)(C) under (ii)(E) (possible until Sept 14, 2028 — could change before Aug 2027!). (b) transfer timing: (f)(8)(i)(G): begin classes within 5 months of program completion (Dec 11, 2027? no Dec 11, 2026) → 5 months = May 11, 2027. Aug 2027 start is more than 5 months after completion → fails (G) even aside from (C). Unless he transfers out by May 11, 2027 (transfer-out date within 5 months)... "begin classes at the transfer school or program within 5 months of transferring out of the current school or within 5 months of the program completion date, whichever is earlier." If he transfers out, say, March 2027 (before completion?) — he must be maintaining status; if he transfers out in March while still enrolled... completing program Dec 11; hmm "whichever is earlier" — earlier of transfer-out or completion date. Aug 2027 start > 5 months after Dec 11, 2026 completion, and > 5 months after any transfer-out before Dec 11. So timing fails regardless. (c) authorized until: program end Dec 11, 2026 + 60 days (transition) = Feb 9, 2027. Compute: Dec 11 + 60: Dec has 20 remaining (Dec 12–31), Jan 31 = 51, +9 → Feb 9, 2027. (d) could change before Aug 2027: (f)(5)(ii)(E) delay/suspension by DHS via FR notification possible until Sept 14, 2028; no notification published as of Nov 14, 2026. Also new NPRMs (OPT fees, grace period) don't change this.

- Q9: five changes between NPRM and final: from V.A list: e.g., (1) 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C) now applies only to programs completed after effective date; (2) new (f)(5)(ii)(E) 2-year limit on delay authority + FR announcement; (3) (f)(5)(v) early-completion 30-day departure clarification + immediate departure for status violators; (4) 214.1(m)(1)(ii)/(iii) reorganization of I-539 exemption; (5) (f)(10)(ii)(D) clarifies OPT via EOS or CBP admission; (6) (f)(11)(i)(D) 60→30 days for reinstatement start date; (7) (f)(5)(viii) title change; (8) 248.1(e) edit. Also earlier in comments: 214.1(c)(5) removal. Cite lines/FR pages: V.A is at 91 FR 45096-45098.

- Q15 item 3: statement about 240 days: "may stay and keep studying but must stop any on-campus job" — per (f)(5)(viii), automatic employment extension max 240 days from I-94 end; after that stop employment; may remain while pending (stay). Correct. But check: does the rule let them stay beyond 240 days while pending? (f)(5)(viii) first sentence: considered in authorized stay until USCIS issues decision (no 240-day limit on stay). Yes. So statement 3 correct.

- Q15 item 2: "counted from the day the student enters the U.S." — incorrect; counted from program start date (f)(5)(i); preamble 15395-97, 15333-338 (page 45015-16).

- Q15 item 1: incorrect — (f)(7)(iii)(B): timely if received on or before expiration of authorized stay incl. 30-day (f)(5)(v) period; but employment consequences if filed in that window. Also "Notwithstanding 214.1(c)(4)..." Actually 214.1(c)(4) requires filing before expiration for... hmm (c)(4) is about extension applications being filed before expiration? The final rule retained (c)(4)? The amendment list didn't touch (c)(4). (f)(7)(iii)(B) last sentence: "Notwithstanding Sec. 214.1(c)(4), USCIS must receive the extension of stay application on or before the expiration of the previously authorized period of stay." So a filed-but-not-received application is not enough. Statement 1 incorrect: deadline is expiration of authorized stay including 30-day grace, not program end date.

- Q15 item 5: partly incorrect: the rule doesn't shorten or require two I-20s; student admitted to 4-year max and must file EOS (f)(5)(i), (f)(7). The preamble at 15454-83 (page 45098-99) acknowledges programs longer than 4 years; requires EOS or depart/re-enter. Actually check: does the NPRM/anything mention issuing "on two I-20s"? No. So statement incorrect.

- Q15 item 6: correct per preamble 15371-77 and 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A); new admission from CBP with I-20 program end + 30 days; then no USCIS EOS needed for that period. Caveat: pending EOS may be deemed abandoned (214.1(c)(8)(ii)); departure while EOS pending nuance. Also note preamble (b) discussion: if admitted for program length, pending EOS considered abandoned. So "correct" with caveat.

- Q15 item 7: incorrect: March 18, 2027 not 6 months from effective date (March 15, 2027); 214.1(m)(1)(i) sets March 18, 2027; (m)(1)(iii) allows 6-month extensions by FR notice; no extension published as of Nov 14, 2026 (searches found none — but I haven't specifically searched for such a notice; the RIN search found only the final rule; a notice would have different RIN but same docket ICEB-2025-0001 — my docket search found only the rule). Good.

- Q3(a): earliest admission: 30 days before program start/report date (Jan 12, 2027): Jan 12 − 30 days = Dec 13, 2026. Show arithmetic. He entered Dec 20, 2026 — within the window.
  Wait — Tomás's program is Jan 12, 2027–Dec 18, 2027 (master's). He entered Dec 20, 2026 — that's 23 days before start. (a) "earliest date on which Tomás could have been admitted for this program" = Dec 13, 2026 (30 days before report date, per (f)(5)(i)).

- Q3(b): I-94 admit-until: program end Dec 18, 2027 + 30 days = Jan 17, 2028. Dec 18 + 30: Dec 13 remaining + 17 → Jan 17, 2028. Yes.

- Q3(e): USCIS must receive application by Jan 17, 2028 (f)(7)(iii)(B). Later filing: if received during the 30-day window it's still timely (that IS the window: Dec 18, 2027–Jan 17, 2028; filing on/before Dec 18 also timely). "Would a later filing still be timely?" — after Jan 17, 2028: not timely for extension; he'd need reinstatement (f)(7)(viii) — actually (f)(7)(viii) covers late DSO SEVIS updates; if his EOS is late → out of status; reinstatement required. Also filing during Dec 18–Jan 17 window: timely but no automatic employment extension (f)(5)(viii).

- Q3(f): automatic extension: 240 days from Jan 17, 2028 → Sept 13, 2028 (approx mid-September 2028). Also (f)(9)/(f)(10) conditions and 274a.12(b)(6)(i),(iii),(c)(3)(iii).

- Q3(g): approved: extension for period necessary to complete program per new I-20 (May 19, 2028) not to exceed 4 years (f)(7)(vi) → until May 19, 2028, plus 30-day departure period → June 18, 2028. May 19 + 30 = June 18. Denied after I-94 expired → must depart immediately (f)(7)(vii).

- Q4(a): Tomás filed I-539 Dec 1, 2027; trip Dec 22–Jan 5. 214.1(c)(8)(i): not abandoned if previously authorized admission hasn't expired at re-entry and he seeks admission for the balance of the period. His admission expires Jan 17, 2028 → OK. Re-entry presentation: (c)(8)(i) — seek admission "for the balance of the previously authorized admission period"; if he instead seeks admission for the full program (new I-20 for later end date — his I-20 now shows May 19, 2028 end date!). Hmm — his DSO issued an I-20 with new program end date May 19, 2028 in Oct 2027. That I-20's program end date is beyond his previously authorized admission (Jan 17, 2028). If he seeks admission with that I-20, (c)(8)(ii): EOS may be deemed abandoned. Tricky! The rule (c)(8)(i) protects departure/re-entry seeking the balance of previously authorized admission. He should carry: I-797C receipt notice + I-20 (c)(8)(iii). The adviser should flag: at the POE he must seek readmission for the balance of the previously authorized period, not a new longer period. This is a nice nuance.
  (b): 248.1(f): COS application abandoned if departs while pending.

- Q7(d): (f)(5)(vii) — cap-gap: automatic extension until April 1 of the fiscal year requested or petition validity start date, whichever earlier. Lena's H-1B start July 1, 2027 — is her petition cap-subject? "section 214(g)(1)(A)" cap-subject requirement; cap-exempt employer → petition not subject to (g)(1)(A) cap → (f)(5)(vii) requires "beneficiary of an H-1B petition subject to section 214(g)(1)(A)". Cap-exempt petitions are not subject to (g)(1)(A) → no automatic extension. Hmm. The question says "a university (a cap-exempt employer) offers her a postdoc and will file an H-1B petition requesting a change of status, with a start date of July 1, 2027." (d): "does any F-1 provision automatically extend her status until the H-1B start date? Cite the current provision." Answer: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vii) (cap-gap) exists, but by its terms applies only to petitions subject to 214(g)(1)(A) (cap-subject) — a cap-exempt petition isn't, so no automatic extension; she must maintain F-1 status (e.g., EOS) until July 1, 2027. Hmm wait — also "timely filed" and start date consistent with (h)(2)(i)(I). Since cap-exempt petitions can be filed anytime, she could file and get approval. The automatic extension provision wouldn't apply. Good nuance.

- Q7(e): travel while COS pending → 248.1(f) (added by 2026-14439): application considered abandoned. (Also 214.1(c)(8) is for EOS, not COS.)

- Q7(a): "the presidential document currently imposing that payment requirement" = Proclamation 11069 (2026-19554, signed Sept 18, 2026, 91 FR 60497-60500), which re-imposes the restriction with $100,000 payment, effective 12:01 a.m. EDT Sept 21, 2026, expires absent extension 12 months after effective date = Sept 21, 2027. Other docs: Proclamation 10973 (2025-18601, 90 FR 46027, signed Sept 19, 2025, effective Sept 21, 2025, expired Sept 21, 2026); EO 14431 (2026-19555, 91 FR 60501, signed Sept 18, 2026) — program integrity/coordination, related but doesn't itself impose payment.
  (b): Payment applies to entry of H-1B workers; restriction applies only to aliens who enter/attempt to enter after effective date; petitions on behalf of aliens outside the U.S. (Sec. 2(a)). Lena is in the U.S. in F-1 with a COS request → her petition doesn't trigger entry restriction; not covered. Could reach her: if she departs and re-enters to effectuate H-1B (consular processing), the restriction applies (2026 Proclamation Sec. 3(a) — applies to aliens who must seek admission to effectuate petition approval); unless national-interest exception (Sec. 1(c)) or payment made.

- Q7(c): DHS rulemakings adding fees for H-1B petitions: 2026-17324 NPRM ($103,265 for cap-subject petitions, payable at filing, proposed 8 CFR 106.2(a)(3)(xii)); would NOT apply to Lena (cap-exempt petitions excluded, INA 214(g)(5),(7)); status: proposed, comments closed Sept 24, 2026; correction C1-2026-17324 (91 FR 57516, Sept 10, 2026) fixed Table 13 data. Also check whether there's an interim final rule or final rule — search found only NPRM. Also the OPT fee NPRM (2026-20660) adds fees but for OPT, not H-1B — mention as related but not H-1B.

- Q10: docs July 18, 2026–Nov 14, 2026 relevant to F-1 post-graduation work:
  1. 2026-19554 (Proclamation 11069, Sept 23, 2026) — extends $100,000 H-1B entry restriction; in force until Sept 21, 2027.
  2. 2026-19555 (EO 14431, Sept 23, 2026) — interagency H-1B scrutiny; in force.

  5. 2026-20955 (final rule, Oct 14, 2026, effective same day) — ends automatic extension of EAD validity for timely renewal applications in certain categories; in force. Need to confirm scope — does it touch F-1/OPT? Grep quickly for "F-1" in 2026-20955.
  6. 2026-18631 (NPRM, Sept 11, 2026) — grace period elimination — matters for students planning to move to H-1B/O-1 etc. (60-day grace on cessation of employment) — NOT in force; comments closed Nov 10, 2026.
  That's ≥4 (actually 6). Need one-sentence summaries + in-force status. Let me check 2026-20955 scope re F-1 quickly.

- Q11: still need figures. Let me grep RIA for cost per application: pattern "I-539" is frequent. Better pattern: "\$[0-9]{2,3}(\.[0-9]{2})? (filing fee|fee)" or "biometric" near fee. In RIA, typical: I-539 fee $470? (2024 fee schedule: I-539 paper $470, online $420; biometrics $85 removed under 2024 fee rule for I-539? Actually 2024 fee rule: I-539 $470 paper/$420 online, no separate biometric fee). Let me grep "\$470|\$420|\$620|\$520" — earlier grep for $470/$420 found only two matches (one $855, one $420 in comment). So the RIA may express costs differently — e.g., "$505" or uses average. Try grep "per-adjudication|per adjudication|cost of adjudicat|fully burdened". Or grep "EOS application.{0,60}\$". Try pattern "I-539 .{0,200}\$" hmm single-line. Grep pattern "\$[0-9]" with max 100 would flood. Try "fee schedule" context 4.

content.text:
2026-20955 doesn't touch F-1 specifically (only a citation and List of Subjects). It amends 274a.12 automatic extensions for renewal EADs (categories like TPS, asylum, etc.). For Q10, I can describe it accurately: finalizes the Oct 30, 2025 IFR ending automatic extension of expired EADs for aliens with timely filed renewals in certain EAD categories; matters to an F-1 student only if they hold or later obtain a category that relied on automatic extension — actually for an F-1 planning post-graduation work, marginal relevance; I'll characterize carefully and note F-1 OPT/STEM not among renewal-based categories (OPT isn't renewed; STEM is a new application). Hmm — but actually, is F-1's 240-day rule in 274a.12(b)(20)/(b)(6)(iv) affected? The rule's CFR affected is 8 CFR 274. I shouldn't overclaim. Let me grep 2026-20955 for which paragraphs amended — grep "274a.12(b)" context. Quick check of regulatory text at end: lines ~7504+. Read lines 7504-7514? The doc is 7514 lines — regulatory text near end. Read 7440-7514.

For Q11, the final rule doesn't state a specific filing fee amount for the EOS in the regulatory text; the preamble says fee = I-539 filing fee as set by USCIS fee schedule (fee-for-service, full cost recovery); commenter noted ~$420/$367/$800 figures. Processing time: DHS "cannot guarantee processing times"; commenters noted ~3.5 months; the rule acknowledges possible increases. So the handout sentence: extension costs = Form I-539 filing fee under USCIS fee schedule (plus possible biometrics under 8 CFR 103.16), and USCIS does not publish a guaranteed processing time in the rule; DHS acknowledges the rule may increase processing times. Also RIA annualized costs $443.1–448.6 million — that's aggregate. For the handout: "An F-1 extension of stay is filed on Form I-539 with the required fee set under USCIS's fee schedule and may require biometrics (8 CFR 214.1(c)(2); 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A)); the final rule sets no fee amount or processing-time guarantee, and DHS acknowledges the rule may increase USCIS processing times (91 FR 45010, 45025)."

Let me read 2026-20955's amended text quickly (last ~70 lines) to state which paragraphs amended.

content.text:
Good: 2026-20955 adopts the Oct 30, 2025 IFR (90 FR 48799) as final — ends automatic EAD extension on timely renewal filings in 274a.12 categories. For F-1 OPT: OPT/STEM I-765s aren't renewals of an existing EAD category; but 274a.12(b)(6)(iv) 180-day STEM extension? Hmm — the 180-day extension while STEM I-765 pending is a form of automatic extension of the OPT EAD. Does 2026-20955 affect it? The IFR targeted renewal categories (TPS, asylum/EEP, etc.). I shouldn't overclaim; the final rule's F-1 grep found no F-1 references except a citation. The preamble of the student rule (2026-14439, 91 FR 45037) states STEM OPT applicants remain eligible for the 180-day extension per 274a.12(b)(6)(iv) — as of July 2026. Whether 2026-20955 (Oct 2026) touched b(6)(iv) — the final rule amended "paragraphs (b)(20)?" I don't know which paragraphs. It says "adopts the amendments ... as published on October 30, 2025, at 90 FR 48799 as final." I can't read the IFR without more calls. I'll describe it as: ends automatic extension of EAD validity upon timely filed renewal applications in the EAD categories covered by the IFR; I could not confirm from the documents read whether F-1's 274a.12(b)(6)(iv) 180-day provision is affected; the rule contains no F-1-specific amendments. Reasonable.

Remaining checks:
1. Q16(b) early filing — grep final rule for discussion of filing window (e.g., "180 days" or "advance"). 
2. Q15 item 4: ELT medical extension — read response ~8081-8140.
3. Q12: whether the preamble addresses filing I-539 in the 60-day transition window / employment. Maybe in Transition comments (5385-5745). Grep "60 day" in transition section? Let me grep "60-day|60 days" context in 5364-5745 region — can't region-restrict. Grep "files? .{0,60}(during|within) the 60" pattern.

content.text:
Line 8619-8624 (91 FR 45043): "shouldn't experience any disruptions if they apply as early as possible (180 days) before the expiration of their current stay." — This is in response about graduate students. So the rule's discussion references filing up to 180 days before expiration as "as early as possible". This is preamble, not regulatory text. For Q16(b): regulatory text sets only the latest receipt date (f)(7)(iii)(B); preamble suggests applying "as early as possible (180 days) before the expiration" (91 FR 45043). So answer: may file up to 180 days before expiration per DHS's discussion; the regulatory text itself sets no minimum earliest date. Good enough.

Now I have nearly everything. Remaining minor: Q1(e) — congressional review. The DATES note: "classified as a major rule subject to congressional review... if the effective date has been changed, DHS will publish..." No subsequent document found. Could a CRA joint resolution disapprove? Search FR for a joint resolution (PRESDOCU? no, resolutions aren't in FR; signed by President as public laws; the FR may publish the President's signing statement as PRESDOCU). Let me do one search: query "Fixed Time Period of Admission" doc_type PRESDOCU since 2026-07-17. Also maybe a DHS notice delaying effective date would have same docket — already searched. Let me do a quick PRESDOCU search.

Also Q2(c) nuance: transfer timing — (f)(8)(i)(G): within 5 months of program completion (May 15, 2027) → Oct 14, 2027; Aug 24, 2027 OK. Also (D)? Also she must be maintaining status; her transition admission ends July 14, 2027 (program end + 60). Transfer release date should be before her admission expires... Actually transfer procedure: transfer-out school sets release date = current semester/session completion date or expected transfer date. Fine.

Also Q2(e) — "What must she file to remain in the U.S. for the OPT period?" She files I-765 (March 1, 2027) — before March 18, 2027 → I-539 exemption (m)(1)(i); no I-539 needed. If approved: remain until EAD expiration (June 13, 2028) + 60 days = Aug 12, 2028.

Q13(b): Sofia departed before filing OPT and was readmitted with fixed admission → (m)(1)(ii): must file both I-765 and I-539. When must USCIS receive I-539? By expiration of her authorized period of admission (June 13, 2027 = May 14 + 30 days). Actually she should file it with/after the I-765; deadline: receipt on or before June 13, 2027. Hmm — but also should it be received before her admission expires; yes June 13, 2027. Let me double check (f)(7)(iii)(B) applies to OPT EOS: (f)(10)(ii)(D) directs to EOS under (f)(7). Yes.

Wait, one more check on Q13(a): after readmission Jan 9, 2027 with same I-20 (program end May 14, 2027): admitted until program end + 30 = June 13, 2027 (214.1(a)(4)(i)(A); (f)(5)(i); preamble 15371-77). Note her previous transition admission (program end + 60) is superseded by new admission. Answer: June 13, 2027.

Q13(d): no travel before filing; files I-765 Feb 22, 2027 (< March 18, 2027) → no I-539 required (m)(1)(i). Travels May 20–June 5 while I-765 pending: (m)(1)(ii): alien who departs while I-765 pending "will be admitted pursuant to paragraph (a)" — 214.1(a)(4)(iii): admitted until EAD end date (if approved) or DSO recommended end date on I-20 (if pending, with receipt notice) + 30 days. Her requested OPT: June 10, 2027–June 9, 2028. So admitted until June 9, 2028 + 30 days = July 9, 2028 (if EAD approved by re-entry with end June 9, 2028, admitted until EAD end + 30 = July 9, 2028). Also (f)(5)(i)(D): period of authorized stay between EAD expiration and I-94 admit-until. Carry: I-797C receipt notice + I-20 endorsed for OPT with recommended end date (214.1(c)(8)(iii); preamble 15365-89). Note caution: she must have EAD in hand if approved (preamble footnote 303).

One nuance for Q13(d): does she need an I-539? Under (m)(1)(i) no I-539 required if filed by March 18, 2027. Departure after filing doesn't trigger (m)(1)(ii) (which applies to students who depart before filing). So no I-539. But is the pending I-765 abandoned by travel? (c)(8)(ii): EOS applications may be deemed abandoned if departure with I-20 for program end beyond authorized admission; corresponding EAD applications not considered abandoned. Her I-765 not abandoned. Good.

Q16(e): husband's I-94 later than Lin's: (f)(5)(i)(E): F-2 authorized stay may not exceed principal's; preamble 5346-5362: dependents must depart when principal departs even if I-94 longer. Until when may he stay? His authorized stay is limited to Lin's — he may not stay beyond Lin's admission (Sept 22, 2031), notwithstanding later I-94. Coverage when Lin applies: include him on her I-539 (214.1(c)(2) family unit filing; (f)(7)(iv) — F-2 must be included or file own; extensions granted for same period; shortest period granted to any member granted to all). Fee: 214.1(c)(2) — family members may be included in one application; fee — the rule: (f)(7)(iv) says "remitting the appropriate fee" for dependents filing their own; if included on principal's application — preamble line 5016-5019: "The Form I-539 allows dependents (non-U.S. citizens) to be included for one fee and concurrent adjudication." And line 6939-41: "dependents may be included in the principal's EOS application for no additional fee if statuses expire simultaneously." Great — cite those (91 FR 45015 & 45029).

Now Q16(b): "what does she submit" — Form I-539 (EOS) with endorsed I-20, evidence of funds, biometrics (8 CFR 103.16), fee (214.1(c)(2); (f)(7)(iii)(A)); ground: (f)(7)(i) — unable to complete program by end of authorized admission + maintained status + full course of study. Husband included per (f)(7)(iv). Early filing: preamble suggests up to 180 days before expiration (91 FR 45043); regulatory text sets no earliest date (only latest: receipt on/before expiration incl. 30-day period (f)(7)(iii)(B)). Granted in full: period necessary to complete program per I-20 (May 14, 2033), not to exceed 4 years (f)(7)(vi) → until May 14, 2033, plus 30-day departure period → June 13, 2033 (I-94 date).

Q16(a): show arithmetic: program start Aug 23, 2027; 4-year max from program start (preamble 15333-338, 15395-97; (f)(5)(i)): Aug 23, 2031; plus 30-day departure period → I-94 admit-until Sept 22, 2031. Aug 23 + 30: Aug 8 remaining (24–31), 22 days into Sept → Sept 22, 2031.

Q16(d): readmitted Aug 2030 on her I-20; no pending EOS. Under preamble 15371-77: admitted for length indicated by program end date not to exceed 4 years, plus 30 days. Program end May 14, 2033. 4-year max counted from program start date (Aug 23, 2027) → Aug 23, 2031; +30 → Sept 22, 2031. So she'd be admitted until Sept 22, 2031 (unchanged), and still needs the I-539 to reach May 14, 2033. Certainty: moderate — the "counted from program start date" method is stated in preamble for initial admissions; its application to mid-program readmissions is not explicit; alternative reading (fresh 4 years from readmission) would run to Aug 2034 — but that would exceed her program end anyway... wait, "whichever is shorter": program length (to May 14, 2033) vs 4 years from readmission (Aug 2034) → shorter = May 14, 2033! Interesting: if 4 years counted from readmission, she'd be admitted until May 14, 2033 (program end, shorter), covering the whole PhD — no EOS needed. So the two readings diverge materially. Which is right? The rule text (f)(5)(i): "admitted for a fixed period of time, which is the period necessary to complete the course of study indicated on the Form I-20, not to exceed a period of 4 years". The preamble's counting rule: 4-year max calculated from program start date. Under that method, her 4 years run from Aug 23, 2027 regardless of readmission → capped at Aug 23, 2031 (+30). The purpose (prevent indefinite stay, periodic DHS review) supports not resetting. Also the transition rule caps at 4 years from effective date regardless of program end — same anti-reset philosophy. I'll answer: admitted until the 4-year maximum measured from her program start date — i.e., admitted period ends Aug 23, 2031, with I-94 until Sept 22, 2031 — and yes she still needs the filing in (b). Certainty: moderately high on outcome (still needs I-539) but flag the ambiguity: the text does not expressly address readmission timing; DHS's stated method (from program start date) is the most defensible reading. Also note (a)(4)(i)(B) second clause explicitly contemplates readmission with I-20 "for a program end date beyond their previously authorized period of admission" → "admitted for the period specified in Sec. 214.2(f)(5)" — (f)(5) caps at 4 years; and the preamble says the 4-year count is from program start date. Also her previously authorized admission (to Sept 22, 2031) hasn't expired when she departs (Aug 2030) — hmm, then what governs? She departs and returns before her admission expires; preamble bullet: aliens who departed without approved EOS, applying with valid I-20 → admitted for program end date not to exceed 4 years + 30 days. CBP could readmit her simply for the balance of her existing admission. Either way, she cannot get past the 4-year cap without an EOS. Conclusion stands.

Now, a few more verifications:
1. Q1(e): check PRESDOCU/any CRA action. Quick search.
2. Q11: verify some cost figures exist in RIA — grep "I-539" in RIA region for fee amounts. The preamble response at 6030-6040: "DHS is authorized to charge fees ... full costs of services" (91 FR 45022). The au pair comment: "$367 to over $800" (commenter statement). Commenter: "$420 fee" (91 FR 45055, re J-1). For the handout, I'll use: Form I-539 fee as prescribed by USCIS fee schedule + possible biometrics; no amount in the rule; DHS can't guarantee processing time; DHS acknowledges potential increase; USCIS data in comments ~3.5 months (commenter statement). Actually, hmm, the question asks "What does the final rule say on these points? Give the figures and where they appear". The figures that appear: $420 (commenter), $367→$800+ (commenter), annualized costs $443.1–$448.6M (RIA, 91 FR 44980, 45083), $233 per EOS request DSO burden (commenter). And processing: no guarantee; encouraged to apply 180 days early (91 FR 45043). I'll present these with correct attribution (preamble/commenter vs. final regulatory text silent).

3. One more check for Q1(e) and any FR notice extending the March 18, 2027 I-539 exemption or delaying (f)(5)(ii) provisions — docket search earlier (ICEB-2025-0001) returned only the final rule. Good.

4. Q10 also should include 2026-14439 itself? No — it's before July 18? Published July 17, 2026 — one day before the window. Excluded; window is July 18–Nov 14. Good.

No CRA-related or effective-date-change documents found. Q1(e): The rule was classified as a major rule subject to congressional review (CRA); effective date Sept 15, 2026, "at the conclusion of the congressional review, if the effective date has been changed, DHS will publish a document in the Federal Register" (91 FR 44976, DATES). As of Nov 14, 2026, no such document appears in the FR; searches of the docket (ICEB-2025-0001) and RIN 1653-AA95 show no correction or notice changing the effective date. It has taken effect (the Sept 2026/Oct 2026 documents reference it as in force? The 60-day grace NPRM published Sept 11 references the proposed rule; the OPT fee NPRM Oct 8 amends 214.2(f)(11) referencing the final rule structure). I can say: it took effect Sept 15, 2026; nothing published since changes that; theoretically it could still change via CRA disapproval or DHS publication, but no such document exists as of Nov 14, 2026.

Also note the rule's own texts embed effective dates (Sept 15, 2026) in 214.1(a)(4) and (m) — evidence it took effect.

Now Q9 needs at least five changes with paragraph + FR location. From 91 FR 45096–45098 (V.A):
1. 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C) limited prospectively (applies only to programs completed after Sept 15, 2026).
2. New 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E): 2-year sunset on DHS authority to delay/suspend transfer/change-of-level provisions + FR announcement requirement.
3. 214.2(f)(5)(v): early-completion departure within 30 days + immediate departure for status violators.
4. 214.1(m)(1)(ii)–(iii): I-539 exemption reorganization; DHS discretion to extend exemption in 6-month increments by FR notice.
5. 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D): OPT students may either file EOS with USCIS or seek CBP admission after travel.
6. 214.2(f)(11)(i)(D): 60→30 days (start date no more than 30 days after program end).
7. 214.1(c)(5) (proposed) removed — USCIS discretion already addressed by 214.1(c)(7).
8. 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A): added examples of extenuating circumstances (elementary/secondary) and clarified graduate-level prohibitions.
9. 8 CFR 248.1(e): removed proposed text re forms accompanying COS approvals.
10. J-1: (j)(1)(vii)(A) employment during pending EOS 240 days; special provision for first six months.

That's plenty. Q9 asks "where in the Federal Register you found the change described" — 91 FR 45096–45098 (2026-14439, section V.A).

Now assemble the final JSON. It's a big answer set (16 questions). I must output pure JSON, no fences. Be thorough but concise. Let me draft each.

Q1:
(a) 2026-14439, 91 FR 44976–45131.
(b) Published July 17, 2026; effective Sept 15, 2026.
(c) Docket DHS Docket No. ICEB-2025-0001; RIN 1653-AA95.
(d) Finalized NPRM 2025-16554, 90 FR 42070, published Aug 28, 2025.
(e) Effective date unchanged as of Nov 14, 2026; rule was major-rule/CRA classified; DATES states if effective date changed DHS will publish a document; searches show no such document; no corrections to the rule. Note: rule's own text hard-codes Sept 15, 2026 in 214.1(a)(4), (m)(1).

Q2:
(a) 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1): authorized to remain until later of EAD expiration (none) or program end date May 15, 2027, not to exceed 4 years from Sept 15, 2026; plus 60-day departure period. May 15, 2027 + 60 days = July 14, 2027. So authorized through July 14, 2027 without filing.
(b) F: Nov 14, 2030 (4 years from Sept 15, 2026 = Sept 15, 2030, + 60 days = Nov 14, 2030 — the rule states this expressly, 214.1(m)(1)); J: Oct 15, 2030 (Sept 15, 2030 + 30 days).
(c) Yes — transfer timing: (f)(8)(i)(G): begin classes within 5 months of transferring out or of the program completion date on current I-20 (May 15, 2027), whichever earlier. Aug 24, 2027 − May 15, 2027 = 3 months 10 days (101 days) ≤ 5 months (Oct 14, 2027 deadline). Also (f)(8)(i)(A): she's below graduate level and beyond her first academic year, so the first-year bar doesn't apply. She must transfer while maintaining status (before her authorized stay ends July 14, 2027 — safest before May 15, 2027 program end).
(d) Yes — I-539 EOS with USCIS: 214.1(m)(1) (transition students needing a new program must apply for EOS per (c)(2)); 214.1(c)(2); 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(D) (change in educational objectives requires EOS); (f)(7)(iii)(A) (form, endorsed I-20, funds, biometrics, fee); (f)(8)(iv) (extension for new program); deadline (f)(7)(iii)(B): received on or before expiration of authorized stay.
(e) I-765 filed March 1, 2027 — on or before March 18, 2027 → I-539 not required (214.1(m)(1)(i)). If approved as requested (EAD June 14, 2027–June 13, 2028): remain until EAD expiration + 60 days = Aug 12, 2028. June 13 + 60 = Aug 12.

Q3:
(a) (f)(5)(i): admitted up to 30 days before report/program start date. Jan 12, 2027 − 30 days = Dec 13, 2026. (He entered Dec 20, within window.)
(b) Program end Dec 18, 2027 + 30 days = Jan 17, 2028 ((f)(5)(i), (v)).
(c) Yes: (f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(i) — unexpected research problems caused by unexpected change in faculty advisor. Not acceptable: delays from academic probation/suspension or repeated inability/unwillingness (same paragraph; also Summary of Changes 91 FR 44979).
(d) DSO issued new I-20 Oct 2027, before Dec 18, 2027 end date → timely; Tomás must file EOS (f)(7). If DSO had entered the new end date after Dec 18, 2027 passed → (f)(7)(viii): late request; student must file reinstatement with USCIS (fee + biometrics); F-2s likewise.
(e) USCIS must receive on or before Jan 17, 2028 (f)(7)(iii)(B). Later filing (during Dec 18, 2027–Jan 17, 2028 grace): still timely but no automatic employment extension — must wait for approval before continuing CPT/on-campus work ((f)(5)(viii), (f)(7)(iii)(B)). After Jan 17, 2028: not timely; out of status; reinstatement route.
(f) 240 days from I-94 end (Jan 17, 2028): Jan 18–31 (14) + Feb 29 + Mar 31 + Apr 30 + May 31 + Jun 30 + Jul 31 + Aug 31 = 227 through Aug 31; +13 → Sept 13, 2028. So approx. through Sept 13, 2028, subject to earlier decision ((f)(5)(viii); 274a.12(b)(6)(i),(iii),(c)(3)(iii) cross-referenced).
(g) Approved: extension for period necessary to complete program per endorsed I-20 (May 19, 2028), not to exceed 4 years (f)(7)(vi) → through May 19, 2028, plus 30-day departure period → I-94/authorized stay to June 18, 2028. Denied after I-94 passed: he and dependents must depart immediately (f)(7)(vii).

Q4:
(a) 214.1(c)(8)(i): EOS not deemed abandoned if at re-entry the previously authorized admission hasn't expired (Jan 17, 2028) and he seeks admission for the balance of the previously authorized period. Presentation matters: if he presents the new I-20 with the later program end date (May 19, 2028) and seeks admission beyond his current admission, (c)(8)(ii) risks deeming the I-539 abandoned (the preamble, 91 FR 45099–45100, explains CBP's new admission supersedes pending EOS). He should travel with the I-797C receipt notice and his I-20 ((c)(8)(iii)); RFE-monitoring caution (preamble 91 FR 45100).
(b) 8 CFR 248.1(f) (added by 2026-14439): a timely filed change-of-status application is deemed abandoned if the alien departs the U.S. while it is pending.

Q5: Mei.
Provisions:
- (f)(8)(i) intro: eligibility to transfer requires maintaining status.
- (f)(8)(i)(B): eligible if (1) pursuing full course of study, (2) completed a degree program, or (3) completing/completed post-completion/STEM OPT. Mei will have completed the master's (May 14, 2027) → (B)(2).
- (f)(8)(i)(C): student not currently in a graduate-level program unless SEVP exception under (f)(5)(ii)(A). While enrolled in the master's (a graduate-level program) she may not transfer; after completion she is no longer "currently in" the program → (C) no longer bars; transfer after May 14, 2027 is available without SEVP exception.
- (f)(5)(ii)(A): graduate-level students may not transfer during program unless SEVP exception — applies while she's in the master's.
- (f)(5)(ii)(B): completed one level, begins higher level → maintaining status: bachelor's→master's earlier and master's→PhD now; supports PhD.
- (f)(5)(ii)(C): bars same/lower level — PhD is higher; not triggered. (Also applies only to programs completed after Sept 15, 2026.)
- (f)(8)(i)(G): begin classes within 5 months of transferring out or program completion (May 14, 2027) → by Oct 14, 2027; Aug 23, 2027 OK.
- (f)(8)(ii)/(iii): transfer procedure; change of education level via transfer procedures.
- 214.1(m)(1): she must file I-539 EOS with USCIS for the PhD admission period (new program start Aug 23, 2027 after her authorized stay ends — May 14, 2027 + 60 = July 13, 2027); (f)(8)(iv): EOS if new program not completed within authorized stay.
Conclusion: Yes — after completing the master's on May 14, 2027 (and no later than the release/transfer mechanics in (f)(8)(ii)), her record can be transferred to School B for the PhD; she must also file an I-539 extension of stay to remain for the PhD because her admission expires before the PhD start. If instead she tried to transfer while still enrolled in the master's, (f)(8)(i)(C)/(f)(5)(ii)(A) would bar it absent a SEVP extenuating-circumstances exception.
Could change: (f)(5)(ii)(E) — until Sept 14, 2028 DHS may delay/suspend (ii)(A)–(C) by FR notification/SEVP announcement; no such notification published as of Nov 14, 2026. The OPT fee NPRM (2026-20660) floats an alternative under which the $70,000 initial fee would re-apply at each higher educational level — doesn't change transfer eligibility but would add cost; still only a proposal.

Q6:
(a) No — (f)(5)(ii)(C): an F-1 who completes a program after Sept 15, 2026 at one level may not maintain/be admitted/be provided F-1 status through a program at the same level; MBA = master's-level = same level. Governs both transfer (f)(8)(i) incorporates (f)(5)(ii)(A)–(D) and (f)(8)(i) eligibility) and readmission (214.1(a)(4)). Only if DHS delays/suspends under (f)(5)(ii)(E) could this change.
(b) (f)(8)(i)(G): must begin classes within 5 months of program completion (Dec 11, 2026) → by May 11, 2027 — an Aug 2027 start fails the timing rule regardless of the level bar; and (f)(8)(i)(H) for OPT students similar.
(c) 214.1(m)(1): program end Dec 11, 2026 + 60-day departure period = Feb 9, 2027.
(d) Yes: (f)(5)(ii)(E) lets DHS delay/suspend (f)(5)(ii)(A)–(C) until Sept 14, 2028 with FR/SEVP announcements at least 30 days before implementation — could restore same-level progression before Aug 2027. No such notification published as of Nov 14, 2026. (The pending NPRMs — 2026-18631, 2026-20660 — do not address this.)

Q7:
(a) Currently: Proclamation 11069, signed Sept 18, 2026, published Sept 23, 2026, 2026-19554, 91 FR 60497–60500; effective 12:01 a.m. EDT Sept 21, 2026; expires absent extension 12 months after effective date — Sept 21, 2027 (Sec. 1(a)). Others: Proclamation 10973 (2025-18601, 90 FR 46027, signed Sept 19, 2025, effective Sept 21, 2025, expired Sept 21, 2026 absent extension); EO 14431 (2026-19555, 91 FR 60501, signed Sept 18, 2026) — H-1B program-integrity/interagency coordination, complements but does not itself impose the payment.
(b) Text: restriction applies to entry as H-1B of aliens whose petitions are not accompanied by $100,000 (Sec. 1(a)); applies only to aliens who enter/attempt to enter after effective date (Sec. 3(a)); DHS to restrict decisions on petitions for H-1B workers "currently outside the United States" (Sec. 1(b)); employers must show payment before filing for aliens outside the U.S. (Sec. 2(a)). Lena is in the U.S. in F-1 requesting change of status — no entry → not covered by the payment requirement. Could reach her: if she departs and must seek admission to effectuate the H-1B (consular processing etc., Sec. 3(a)) — then payment or a national-interest exception (Sec. 1(c)) needed.
(c) Yes: 2026-17324 NPRM "Fee for Certain H-1B Petitions" (91 FR 54817, Aug 25, 2026): proposes $103,265 fee, payable at filing, at 8 CFR 106.2(a)(3)(xii), for all H-1B cap-subject petitions (including advanced-degree-exemption) in addition to other fees. Would NOT apply to Lena: proposal expressly excludes cap-exempt petitions under INA 214(g)(5),(7) (91 FR 54819, 54831–32). Status: proposed only; comments closed Sept 24, 2026; corrected by C1-2026-17324 (91 FR 57516, Sept 10, 2026 — Table 13 receipt data). Not in force. (Also note 2026-20660 proposes OPT fees but not H-1B fees.)
(d) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vii) (redesignated cap-gap): automatic extension of status/EAD until April 1 of the fiscal year requested or petition start date, whichever earlier — but by its terms only for petitions "subject to section 214(g)(1)(A)" (cap-subject), timely filed, start date consistent with (h)(2)(i)(I), nonfrivolous. A cap-exempt petition is not subject to (g)(1)(A), so no automatic extension for Lena; she must independently maintain F-1 status (e.g., EOS if needed) until July 1, 2027. F-2 dependents covered only via (f)(5)(vii)(D) when it applies.
(e) 8 CFR 248.1(f): deemed abandoned upon departure while pending (added by 2026-14439).

Q8:
(a) 2026-18631 NPRM (91 FR 57807, Sept 11, 2026), docket CIS No. 2858-26/USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22: would remove 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) — the up-to-60-day grace period following cessation of employment for aliens in certain employment-based nonimmigrant classifications (E-1, E-2, E-3, H-1B, etc., and dependents).
(b) Status: proposed rule; written comments due Nov 10, 2026; not final/in force as of Nov 14, 2026.
(c) Does not affect Priya's 60 days: her 60-day departure period comes from the D/S transition rule 214.1(m)(1) (program-end + 60 days), not 214.1(l)(2); the NPRM's own text discusses F-1's separate departure grace ((f)(5)(iv) pre-rule numbering) only as contrast (91 FR 57814).
(d) Bears on students who leave F-1 for employment-based statuses (e.g., Lena via H-1B, or any student later in H/L/E/O/TN status) who stop working: if finalized, no 60-day grace on cessation of employment. It does not touch the F-1 program-end grace periods in (f)(5)(v)/(m)(1) for the other students (Priya, Sofia, Daniel, Ahmed, Mei, Lin, Tomás).

Q9: list as above.

Q10: six documents as above with status.

Q11: as discussed.

Q12:
(a) Yes — for a transition student under 214.1(m)(1), the authorized period of stay runs to the later of EAD expiry or program end date, plus the 60-day departure period; (f)(7)(iii)(B) makes an EOS timely if received on or before expiration of the authorized period of stay. Receipt during the 60 days (Feb 2027 etc.) is within her authorized stay → timely. Caveat: (f)(7)(iii)(B) literally references "the 30-day period provided in (f)(5)(v)"; for transition students the operative departure period is the 60-day (m)(1) period "as provided in their previous admission" (preamble 91 FR 45101–02), so the most defensible reading is that the 60-day window counts as part of the authorized stay. Uncertainty: the rule never expressly says the 60-day transition window is an EOS filing window.
(b) The automatic-employment-extension bar in (f)(5)(viii) applies only to applications "filed during the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)". Priya filing in the transition 60-day window is not filing during a (f)(5)(v) 30-day period; on the text, the bar should not apply, so she would keep the automatic extension of on-campus/CPT employment (up to 240 days from her I-94 end date). But this is not free from doubt — the rule does not expressly address employment during a transition-window filing; recommend filing before the program end date to eliminate the risk.
Recommendation: file the I-539 (and I-765) before May 15, 2027 program end; if forced to file in the 60-day window it is timely, but employment continuation during pendency is textually uncertain.

Q13:
(a) Readmission Jan 9, 2027 → new fixed admission per 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)/(f)(5)(i): until program end May 14, 2027 + 30 days = June 13, 2027. (Her prior transition 60-day arrangement is superseded by the new admission; preamble 91 FR 45099: aliens departing after effective date get a new fixed admission period.)
(b) Yes — (m)(1)(ii): because she departed before filing OPT and was readmitted with a fixed admission, she must file both I-765 and I-539 ((f)(11)(i)(B)(2)/(C) as cited therein); USCIS must receive the I-539 on or before expiration of her authorized admission — June 13, 2027 ((f)(7)(iii)(B)); practically file together with the I-765 (Feb 22, 2027) — that also works since it's before June 13.
(c) OPT EAD to June 9, 2028 → remain until EAD expiration + 60 days = Aug 8, 2028 (June 9 + 60: June 21 remaining + 31 July = 52 + 8 = Aug 8).
(d) No I-539 — I-765 filed Feb 22, 2027, before March 18, 2027 → (m)(1)(i) exemption. Departure while I-765 pending: admitted under 214.1(a)(4)(iii) — until the DSO's recommended employment end date (June 9, 2028) if the I-765 is still pending, or the EAD end date if approved — plus 30 days → July 9, 2028. Carry: I-797C receipt notice confirming I-765 receipt + endorsed I-20 with recommended end date (214.1(c)(8)(iii); preamble 91 FR 45099); if approved, EAD in hand (footnote 303 caution).

Q14:
(a) 2026-20660 "Optional Practical Training Fees" NPRM, 91 FR 64566–64600, published Oct 8, 2026; ICE/DHS; docket ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01; proposed (not in force); comment deadline Nov 9, 2026; PRA information-collection comments by Dec 7, 2026; proposes final rule effective 60 days after publication (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3)).
(b) $30,000: STEM OPT extension is a "subsequent OPT" — a DSO recommendation for a student who has previously participated in OPT and paid $70,000 (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2); 91 FR 64577 lines 1664–1683). The final regulatory text never fixes a dollar amount; it requires the applicant to file 'the form and in the manner designated by USCIS... and remitting the appropriate fee,' plus evidence of funds and any biometrics required by 8 CFR 103.16 (8 CFR 214.1(c)(2); 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A), 91 FR 45123, 45126). Dollar figures that do appear are in comments, not regulatory text: a commenter put the I-539 filing fee at $420 (91 FR 45055), and another estimated an affected au-pair program's cost rising 'from $367 to over $800' with filing fees and biometrics (91 FR 45056). The rule sets no decision deadline and no service-level target: 'DHS cannot guarantee processing times for applications filed at USCIS due to numerous governing factors' (91 FR 45025), while acknowledging the rule 'may cause an increase in USCIS processing times' (91 FR 45010, 45021) and encouraging nonimmigrants to 'apply well in advance of the expiration of their stay' — the rule's discussion uses about 180 days before expiration as 'as early as possible' (91 FR 45021, 45043).
